paragraphs: The paper presents a processor architecture designed to accelerate machine learning through many arithmetic units working in parallel. These vector processing elements support variable arithmetic resolution. They operate in groups that execute the same instruction on different data, allowing the hardware to perform many related calculations at once.

Each group has its own memory bank, so adding processing elements also increases available memory bandwidth. This matters because arithmetic units need a matching supply of data to remain useful. Keeping the main data transfers local also helps limit power dissipation, connecting the memory design directly to the architecture’s intended efficiency.

A system with 256 processing elements across two FPGA chips sustains 19 billion multiply-accumulate operations per second for SVM training and 86 billion for classification. The reported performance exceeds earlier FPGA implementations by more than an order of magnitude. On MNIST, one FPGA achieves speeds comparable to published GPU results despite a sixfold lower clock rate. These findings motivate embedded applications; tests with other learning algorithms were still underway.
neurips-2008-a-massively-parallel-digita.tldr: A parallel processor architecture combines local memory and many arithmetic units to deliver high SVM throughput at low clock rates.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to assess whether gene expression is conserved across species when the measurements come from complex, heterogeneous datasets. Earlier probabilistic approaches had succeeded in simpler organisms such as yeast, where measurements were typically single values treated as independent. Diverse tissues from more complex organisms create a broader modeling challenge.

The authors introduce a statistical mixture model that extends previous expression-evolution models to handle this setting. Its purpose is to characterize changes in expression among complex organisms while accommodating the non-homogeneous nature of the data. The central contribution is therefore a modeling framework suited to comparisons involving richer biological measurements.

The method is demonstrated on microarray measurements covering multiple tissues and vertebrate species. This application supports its usefulness for studying expression evolution in the setting it was designed to address. Human and mouse help motivate the work because of their scientific and medical relevance. The authors also anticipate applications to organisms such as worms and insects, presenting that broader usefulness as a prospect rather than a demonstrated result.
neurips-2008-a-mixture-model-for-the-evo.tldr: A mixture model extends gene-expression evolution analysis to heterogeneous measurements across tissues and vertebrate species.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak classifiers into a stronger decision procedure. The paper revisits a martingale boosting method that organizes weak classifiers into a branching program and can be analyzed through random walks. The earlier method could tolerate random classification noise when paired with a noise-tolerant weak learner, but did not effectively exploit differences in classifier quality.

The proposed variant makes that quality variation part of the algorithm’s behavior. In its random-walk analysis, the step size changes according to the quality of the weak learner at each stage. This provides the mechanism for adaptiveness: stronger and weaker contributions need not be treated as though they offer the same amount of progress.

The authors prove that the resulting booster is adaptive and requires polynomially fewer weak-learner calls than its predecessor. It also accepts confidence-rated hypotheses with real-valued outputs, extending beyond Boolean predictions. The method retains the earlier noise-tolerance property in the setting involving a noise-tolerant weak learner. Together, these results improve how the booster uses both the quality and the expressive form of its inputs.
neurips-2008-adaptive-martingale-boostin.tldr: An adaptive martingale booster adjusts to weak-learner quality while reducing learner calls and retaining conditional noise tolerance.

paragraphs: Lasso fits a regression model using a penalty that encourages some coefficients to become zero. This yields a sparse solution and provides a form of variable selection. The paper considers how to solve this problem when observations arrive sequentially, so the desired fitted model changes whenever a new data point becomes available.

The authors introduce an optimization problem that connects the existing solution to the solution incorporating the new observation. Their algorithm computes a homotopy, meaning a path between these two fitted solutions. The key idea is to make the transition itself the computational object, using the current fit as the starting point for processing an additional observation.

The method is compared with Lars and applied to compressed sensing with sequential measurements. The same approach can also be extended to remove an observation, tracing a path from the current fit to the fit without that point. This removal operation gives an efficient route to leave-one-out cross-validation, where each observation is excluded in turn to assess the fitted model.
neurips-2008-an-homotopy-algorithm-for-t.tldr: A homotopy algorithm updates Lasso solutions as observations arrive and extends to efficient leave-one-out cross-validation.

paragraphs: A model can leave variation unexplained because its description is inadequate or because the observations contain intrinsic noise. The usual percentage of variance explained mixes these issues and can therefore give a biased assessment of model quality. This paper develops an analytical correction aimed at estimating the underlying variance explained by a model class.

The revised estimator accounts for uncertainty in the estimated noise level, adjusts for overfitting associated with free parameters, and includes a conditioning term. Accounting for fitted parameters mitigates the need for a separate validation dataset. The authors report substantially improved accuracy in terms of bias, with similar or better mean-square error, so reducing bias does not come with a reported deterioration in that error measure.

The estimator is applied to binocular disparity tuning curves from macaque V1 neurons, using Gabor functions as the model class. At the population level, almost all variation left unexplained by those functions is attributed to noise. This changes the interpretation of the residual variation: in this application, much of it does not indicate a shortcoming of the fitted functional description.
neurips-2008-an-improved-estimator-of-va.tldr: A corrected variance-explained estimator separates model performance from noise more accurately while accounting for noise uncertainty and overfitting.

paragraphs: The paper examines how people respond when sensory cues disagree. It builds on a mixture-model approach to describing interactions between conflicting cues. The goal is to understand which versions of that approach best account for observed responses, making the assumptions about sensory uncertainty an explicit part of the investigation.

The authors compare formulations that differ in two respects: how they model sensory noise and how they perform inference. They assess these alternatives by their fit to experimental data. Heavy-tailed sensory likelihoods describe the subjects’ behavior better than standard Gaussian noise models. Such likelihoods allow more probability for large deviations, so this comparison concerns how the model represents unusual sensory observations.

The study also investigates why the heavy-tailed formulations provide the better fit and develops several testable predictions. This moves the contribution beyond choosing a model solely by its agreement with existing responses. The predictions provide ways to examine the models further, while the reported empirical conclusion remains specifically about their description of behavior in the data studied.
neurips-2008-characterizing-response-beh.tldr: Mixture models with heavy-tailed sensory noise better describe observed responses to conflicting cues than Gaussian alternatives.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a center-based clustering algorithm that can work with an arbitrary collection of distances. It begins by expressing clustering as an NP-hard integer linear program, then uses linear programming and duality to develop an efficient algorithm. The computation operates in the dual domain, using a related optimization representation to guide clustering decisions.

Choosing cluster centers is the central design problem. The authors define an LP-based quantity called stability to assess centers, and introduce another quantity called a margin. Margins act roughly as dual counterparts to stabilities and make it possible to approximate them efficiently. These quantities connect the practical choice of centers to the underlying optimization formulation.

The algorithm is independent of initialization and has guaranteed convergence. It also supplies optimality bounds during computation, giving information about the quality of the estimated solution. Convergence and quality bounds are distinct from a claim that every result solves the original NP-hard problem exactly. Experiments are described as promising, supporting the method’s potential alongside its stated algorithmic properties.
neurips-2008-clustering-via-lp-based-sta.tldr: An LP-based clustering method uses center stability and dual margins to guide clustering with convergence guarantees and solution-quality bounds.

paragraphs: This paper adapts a language model for automatic speech recognition using correlated bigram latent semantic analysis. Unigram modeling captures individual-word information, while bigram modeling also represents adjacent word pairs. The proposed approach combines both forms of information for unsupervised adaptation of an existing N-gram language model.

Training uses variational expectation-maximization. The authors also propose fractional Kneser-Ney smoothing to handle the fractional counts produced by the modeling process. To support larger training collections, they describe bootstrapping the bigram model from a unigram model. The two models enter the background language model differently: unigram information through marginal adaptation and bigram information through linear interpolation.

On the Mandarin RT04 test set, using both forms of LSA produces a 6–8% relative perplexity reduction compared with unigram LSA alone. It also lowers character error rate by 0.6 percentage points against that comparison and by 1.2 percentage points against the unadapted baseline. These results show that the added bigram information improves both language-model prediction and the reported speech-recognition outcome in this evaluation.
neurips-2008-correlated-bigram-lsa-for-u.tldr: Combining unigram and correlated bigram LSA improves unsupervised language-model adaptation on a Mandarin speech-recognition test.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Zell, a clustering algorithm intended for complex data containing multiple distributions and scales. It represents the data with a similarity graph and begins with small clusters formed from local links. The distinctive idea is to describe a cluster through the cycles contained in its associated portion of the graph.

A graph zeta function combines information from those cycles into a structural descriptor expressed through a determinant. The authors then define cluster popularity by combining changes in this descriptor when individual members are left out. Clustering proceeds by repeatedly merging the pair of clusters with the largest increase in popularity, linking local graph structure to the overall merging process.

Experiments on artificial data, imagery, and sensory data are reported as promising. On the FRGC face dataset, containing 16,028 samples and 466 facial clusters, the reported normalized mutual information is 98.1%. This is a clustering-agreement measure, so the figure should be understood in that sense. The findings support the potential of cycle-based structure as a guide for assembling larger clusters.
neurips-2008-cyclizing-clusters-via-zeta.tldr: Zell clusters data by merging graph-based groups according to a popularity measure derived from their cycle structure.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to regularize deep neural networks for visual recognition. The authors identify a difficulty with controlling network parameters: restrictions on those parameters need to translate into meaningful control over the function the network computes. Their objective is to make the training constraint informative about the recognition task itself.

The proposed strategy draws on kernel methods. An existing kernel function supplies useful prior knowledge about the task, and the training approach uses that knowledge to guide the neural network. This connects a representation of prior knowledge already available through the kernel with the process of learning the network’s behavior.

The authors derive an efficient algorithm based on stochastic gradient descent and report very positive results across a wide range of visual recognition tasks. The contribution therefore combines a rationale for regularization with a practical training method and empirical demonstrations. Its premise is that a useful task-related kernel is available: that kernel supplies the information intended to make regularization more meaningful than a constraint considered only at the level of network parameters.
neurips-2008-deep-learning-with-kernel-r.tldr: Kernel-based prior knowledge guides regularization of deep visual-recognition networks through an efficient stochastic-gradient training method.

paragraphs: Multi-level hierarchical models describe responses whose relationships follow a hierarchy. Observations linked through that hierarchy can be correlated, and the model incorporates those connections when fitting the data. The paper addresses the computational difficulty that arises when the hierarchy contains many nodes and the posterior mode must be found efficiently.

The authors propose an algorithm based on a multi-scale Kalman filter, describing it as scalable and easy to implement. Its role is to make fitting these structured models more manageable as the hierarchy grows. The algorithm is paired with attention to an estimation issue: for non-Gaussian responses, using a quadratic approximation to the log-likelihood produces biased estimates.

To address that bias, the paper suggests a bootstrap correction strategy. The computational approximation and the correction serve complementary purposes: one supports tractable fitting, while the other addresses distortion introduced in the non-Gaussian case. Simulation studies and applications to healthcare and online advertising illustrate the method, showing its use in both controlled examples and real datasets with hierarchical modeling needs.
neurips-2008-fast-computation-of-posteri.tldr: A multi-scale Kalman-filter algorithm accelerates hierarchical model fitting, with a proposed bootstrap correction for non-Gaussian approximation bias.

paragraphs: Many kernel methods repeatedly add Gaussian contributions from data points, making these summations a computational bottleneck. This paper develops a fast summation algorithm for high-dimensional data. It targets both the number of calculations involved in approximation and the cost of computing individual distances between points.

The method extends multipole-style approximation to accommodate both hard and probabilistic error criteria. It also introduces a subspace tree, whose nodes represent their data through lower-dimensional mappings obtained with a linear dimension-reduction method such as PCA. These mappings reduce the cost of pairwise distance calculations, which the authors identify as a dominant expense in many kernel methods.

The algorithm provides a probabilistic relative-error guarantee for each kernel sum. That means its stated accuracy control is probabilistic and applies to the individual sums, rather than asserting error-free computation. Empirical speedups are reported across datasets ranging from low dimensionality to 89 dimensions. The contribution connects that accuracy control with a data structure designed to reduce a particularly expensive part of high-dimensional computation.
neurips-2008-fast-high-dimensional-kerne.tldr: A Monte Carlo multipole method uses lower-dimensional tree representations to accelerate Gaussian sums with probabilistic relative-error guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper develops time-series classifiers from hierarchical Bayesian generative models, also called mixed-effect models. Its focus is longitudinal data whose sequences may have different lengths and observation times. A Fisher kernel turns information from the fitted generative model into a way of comparing sequences for classification.

The central advance is being able to compute the Fisher information matrix despite those irregular sequences. Replacing that matrix with the identity is a common shortcut, but the authors explain that it discards the geometric basis of the kernel. Their construction preserves that basis, so the resulting kernel is invariant to changes in coordinates used to express the model parameters.

This invariance means that changing the parameter representation does not improperly change the kernel’s comparison of data. The method therefore connects a practical treatment of unevenly sampled sequences with a principled kernel construction. In experiments detecting cognitive decline, classifiers using the proposed kernel outperform classifiers based on the generative models and other feature-extraction routines, supporting its practical value in that application.
neurips-2008-hierarchical-fisher-kernels.tldr: Hierarchical Fisher kernels preserve model geometry for irregular longitudinal data and improve cognitive-decline classification in reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper introduces MeanNN, an approach for estimating information-theoretic quantities from data samples. These include differential entropy, mutual information, and divergence, which describe uncertainty, dependence, and differences between distributions. The distinguishing property is that its estimates are smooth, differentiable functions of the samples and have a clear geometric interpretation.

Smoothness matters when an estimate is used inside an optimization problem. If the data representation changes during learning, a differentiable estimate provides a way to calculate how the objective changes with it. The authors use this property for independent component analysis, developing a smooth expression for mutual information that can be optimized analytically with gradient-descent methods.

The resulting ICA algorithm is evaluated on standard tests, where the authors report improved performance relative to state-of-the-art techniques. The contribution thus links an estimator’s mathematical form to its practical usefulness in learning: MeanNN supplies an information measure that can also guide optimization. The stated empirical improvement concerns the proposed ICA method, while the estimation framework itself covers several information-theoretic quantities.
neurips-2008-ica-based-on-a-smooth-estim.tldr: MeanNN provides smooth information-theoretic estimates that enable gradient-based ICA and yield improved performance on reported standard tests.

paragraphs: Causal analysis becomes difficult when separate datasets record overlapping but different sets of variables. Some variables may connect datasets, while others appear in only one. The paper addresses how to combine causal information learned locally without requiring every dataset to contain the same complete collection of measurements.

The authors introduce ION, a procedure with an asymptotic correctness guarantee. It extracts all structural information obtainable from the marginal independence relations. These relations describe independence within the observed subsets of variables, so the contribution concerns how much causal structure can be recovered by bringing those pieces of information together.

The scope of the guarantee matters: it is about information supported by those independence relations, and correctness is stated asymptotically. It does not assert that any collection of overlapping datasets uniquely identifies a complete causal structure. The authors compare ION’s accuracy with Structural EM and with inference using complete, unified data on simulated and real examples. These comparisons examine both an existing heuristic and the setting where the variables are observed together.
neurips-2008-integrating-locally-learned.tldr: ION combines causal information across overlapping datasets with an asymptotic guarantee covering structure supported by marginal independences.

paragraphs: This paper presents a hierarchical probabilistic model that learns motion structure from natural movies. Its first hidden layer forms a sparse image representation using local amplitude and phase variables. The second layer learns relationships among the phase variables as they change over time, allowing temporal structure to build on the image representation.

After training, the upper-layer units capture patterns of phase shifts in the lower layer. They respond selectively to a moving pattern’s speed and direction while remaining invariant to its orientation and spatial frequency. This gives a specific meaning to transformational invariance here: the representation preserves information about movement across changes in these aspects of the pattern’s spatial structure.

The variety of learned units provides testable predictions about representations that might occur in visual areas V1 and MT. These are proposed biological predictions, rather than a claim that the learned units have been identified in those areas. The model also shows how inference in a graphical model can produce feedback, allowing higher-level representations to influence lower-level ones.
neurips-2008-learning-transformational-i.tldr: A two-layer probabilistic model learns motion representations selective for speed and direction but invariant to orientation and spatial frequency.

paragraphs: An ROC curve describes how a test or scoring rule distinguishes between two groups as its decision threshold varies. A curve estimated from data also carries sampling uncertainty. This paper focuses on representing that uncertainty through confidence bands, so an assessment of the scoring rule includes more than the estimated curve alone.

The authors investigate bootstrap procedures for constructing those bands. Their proposed smoothed bootstrap resamples from a smoothed version of the empirical distribution. This changes the distribution used to generate resampled data, making smoothing part of the uncertainty-estimation procedure rather than simply a way to alter the appearance of the displayed ROC curve.

The paper presents both theoretical arguments and simulation results supporting the smoothed bootstrap over a naive bootstrap for accurate confidence bands. The practical contribution is guidance on how to resample when the object of interest is an entire ROC curve. Its findings concern the quality of uncertainty assessment around that curve, rather than an improvement to the underlying test or scoring rule itself.
neurips-2008-on-bootstrapping-the-roc-cu.tldr: Theory and simulations support a smoothed bootstrap over naive resampling for constructing accurate ROC confidence bands.

paragraphs: Singular value decomposition is used in many machine learning methods, but its computational expense can make exact calculation impractical for very large datasets. The paper introduces QUIC-SVD as a fast approximation to the full decomposition. Its aim is to make this underlying operation more scalable for methods that depend on it.

The approach automatically adjusts sample size using empirical information and provides empirical relative-error control. Sample sizing matters because it determines how much work the approximation performs. By choosing that size automatically, the method seeks to avoid unnecessary sampling while keeping approximation quality under observation. The authors distinguish this combination from earlier Monte Carlo approaches that did not address the full SVD.

Empirical tests show speedups of several orders of magnitude compared with exact SVD. These findings establish a substantial computational advantage in the reported evaluations, while the error control is explicitly empirical. The authors argue that this scalability should support a broad range of methods and applications, treating that wider reach as an expected consequence of accelerating a common computational operation.
neurips-2008-quic-svd-fast-svd-using-cos.tldr: QUIC-SVD approximates the full SVD with adaptive sample sizing and empirical error control, achieving large speedups in reported tests.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression when input features may be disturbed. Instead of considering only the observed feature values, robust regression accounts for disturbances described by an uncertainty set. The authors show that this feature-wise formulation leads to tractable convex optimization problems, making the robustness objective computationally usable.

For one particular uncertainty set, the robust problem is equivalent to Lasso, the regression method that uses an absolute-value penalty on coefficients. This supplies a robustness interpretation of that penalty: under the specified disturbance model, it corresponds to protecting the regression against uncertain features. The equivalence depends on the chosen uncertainty set, rather than applying indiscriminately to every disturbance model.

The authors then consider more general uncertainty sets, obtaining further tractable convex regression formulations. This turns assumptions about disturbances into a way to design learning methods. They also use the robustness perspective to establish sparsity properties of Lasso and a general consistency result covering robust regression problems, including Lasso. The contribution therefore links algorithm design and theoretical properties through a shared treatment of uncertainty.
neurips-2008-robust-regression-and-lasso.tldr: Lasso is equivalent to robust regression under a particular feature-disturbance set, connecting regularization, sparsity, and consistency through robustness.

paragraphs: Compressive sensing combines measurement and compression by acquiring a sparse or compressible signal through a reduced collection of linear measurements. This paper extends that framework to signals that have a concise graphical-model representation. The focus is on sparse signals whose nonzero coefficients occur in clusters, so their arrangement contains useful structure.

The authors use Markov random fields to represent that clustered structure and introduce a reconstruction algorithm called Lattice Matching Pursuit, or LaMP. The model describes more than which coefficients may be nonzero: it captures relationships among them. Incorporating those relationships gives reconstruction a way to exploit the organization of the signal as well as its sparsity.

The paper reports stable recovery of signals modeled by the MRF using many fewer measurements and computations than the state-of-the-art algorithms considered. The relevant scope is the modeled signal class, where clustered nonzero coefficients provide additional information. The result shows the value of matching the reconstruction method to that structure: a suitable graphical description can reduce both the data acquisition burden and the computation required for recovery.
neurips-2008-sparse-signal-recovery-usin.tldr: LaMP exploits MRF-modeled clustering of nonzero coefficients to recover sparse signals with fewer measurements and computations.

paragraphs: The paper presents a spike feature-extraction algorithm aimed at real-time spike sorting. Feature extraction supplies the representation used by the sorting process, so its speed and usefulness directly affect the larger task. The design also targets implementation on a small microchip, making hardware suitability part of the research objective.

The algorithm is evaluated using both synthesized waveforms and experimentally recorded sequences. These two forms of evaluation examine its behavior on constructed inputs and recorded data. Compared with many spike-sorting approaches, the authors report improved speed and accuracy. They also state that the algorithm supports unsupervised execution, addressing how the method can operate as well as how well it performs.

A preliminary hardware implementation uses an integrated microchip connected to a personal computer. This provides an implementation step beyond evaluating the algorithm alone, while retaining the preliminary status of the hardware result. The contribution brings together feature extraction, real-time processing goals, and a path toward miniaturization, with the reported comparisons supporting the algorithm’s computational and sorting performance.
neurips-2008-spike-feature-extraction-us.tldr: A spike feature-extraction method reports improved speed and accuracy and includes a preliminary microchip implementation for real-time sorting.

paragraphs: This paper considers binary classification with a third available action: abstaining from a decision. The optimal Bayes rule in this setting uses two thresholds on posterior probabilities. Those thresholds determine when a class prediction is appropriate and when the classifier should instead reject the observation.

Starting from goals of consistency and sparsity, the authors derive a double hinge loss. It focuses probability estimation near the thresholds that govern the optimal decision rule. This makes the learning objective responsive to the decisions the classifier actually needs to make, concentrating attention on the probability regions where the choice between predicting and abstaining changes.

For suitable kernel machines, the authors prove universal consistency. They also express loss minimization as a quadratic program resembling the standard SVM optimization problem and propose an active-set method for efficient solution. Preliminary experiments illustrate the approach’s usefulness. The contribution combines a decision-based construction of the loss with a computational formulation, while the consistency claim remains explicitly tied to suitable choices of kernel machine.
neurips-2008-support-vector-machines-wit.tldr: A double hinge loss enables SVM-style classification with abstention and is universally consistent for suitable kernel machines.

paragraphs: The Gaussian Process Density Sampler is a generative model for estimating an unknown probability density within a nonparametric Bayesian framework. It constructs the density by transforming a function drawn from a Gaussian process prior. This connects uncertainty about the density to a prior over functions rather than selecting one fixed density shape in advance.

The model is exchangeable, meaning that the ordering of observations does not determine their joint distribution. Its generated samples are consistent with exact, independent sampling from a fixed density produced by the construction. This sampling property concerns the generative model and is distinct from the procedure used to infer the density after observing data.

For inference, the authors use Markov chain Monte Carlo to obtain posterior samples of density functions and predictive samples in the data space. The method can also infer Gaussian-process hyperparameters. Comparisons with existing techniques on a toy problem and a skull-reconstruction task demonstrate its application. The output includes uncertainty over possible densities as well as a distribution for future observations.
neurips-2008-the-gaussian-process-densit.tldr: The Gaussian Process Density Sampler supports Bayesian density estimation through a GP-based generative construction and MCMC inference.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the Markov Indian buffet process, a probability distribution over a potentially infinite collection of binary Markov chains. Each chain represents a hidden quantity that can change between two states over time. The process extends the Indian buffet process so that hidden variables can have temporal dependencies.

The authors use this construction to form a nonparametric version of the factorial hidden Markov model. The potentially infinite collection provides a way to represent an unfixed number of hidden chains, while their Markov structure retains dependence across time. These two aspects belong together: flexibility in the collection of hidden variables is combined with a model of how those variables evolve.

To perform inference, the paper develops a scheme combining slice sampling and dynamic programming. This supplies a computational procedure for working with the proposed model, alongside its probabilistic definition. The authors demonstrate its use for blind source separation, illustrating how temporally evolving hidden components can be used in a task that seeks to separate underlying sources from observations.
neurips-2008-the-infinite-factorial-hidd.tldr: A Markov extension of the Indian buffet process creates a factorial hidden Markov model with a potentially infinite collection of binary chains.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a Bayesian factor regression model that represents uncertainty about both the number of factors and their relationships. Factors are hidden components used to describe the observed data. Treating their number as uncertain allows the model to consider different possible latent descriptions rather than requiring one fixed factor count.

The construction combines a sparse variant of the Indian buffet process with a hierarchical model based on Kingman’s coalescent. The first component provides the sparse, nonparametric factor framework, while the second represents relationships among factors. The hierarchy therefore makes the organization of the hidden components part of the model, alongside their presence.

The authors apply the method to factor analysis and factor regression in gene-expression data. These applications place the same modeling approach in both the analysis of latent variation and the regression setting. The central contribution is the joint treatment of factor complexity and factor relationships: uncertainty concerns how many hidden components are needed and how those components are organized, rather than only the values of parameters within a predetermined structure.
neurips-2008-the-infinite-hierarchical-f.tldr: A nonparametric Bayesian factor model combines sparse factor structure with a hierarchy to represent uncertainty in factor count and relationships.
